openingProblem.problem: In 1949 West German living standards were back at pre-1914 levels. By 1960 industrial production had more than doubled and West Germany was one of the world's biggest traders. Who gained from the 'economic miracle', and who was left out?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: did the economic miracle make West Germany more equal?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: The social market economy and the 'economic miracle'
chunks.body:
When the Federal Republic was founded in 1949, living standards in western Germany had fallen to pre-1914 levels, with food shortages and a black market. The new government's main economic aim was recovery, and its chosen instrument was Ludwig Erhard's **social market economy**. In Geoff Layton's words, it aimed to combine "political and economic freedom with social justice and security": private property and enterprise would be encouraged, but a strong state could intervene to protect the common interests of individuals. Erhard saw it as a "third way" between unrestrained capitalism and an over-regulated socialist economy.

Recovery was uneven at first. In 1951 more than two million West Germans were unemployed, over 10 per cent of the workforce. But by the end of 1951 output had regained pre-war levels, and by 1955 unemployment had fallen to about one million and gross national product had doubled. By 1960 industrial production was more than twice the level of 1950, and West Germany was the world's third biggest trading power. This was the **Wirtschaftswunder**, the "economic miracle".

The "social" side mattered too. The **Co-determination Law** of 1951 put workers' representatives on the boards of iron, coal and steel companies, and the Works' Constitution Law of 1952 created works councils in large firms. Unions and employers worked as partners. Judt adds that the state itself owned or controlled large parts of industry and banking, and that conflict was rare because "the economic cake grew fast enough".

Historians debate the causes. Layton and Mary Fulbrook stress the help of the **Marshall Plan**, which gave Germany more than $1.5 billion. But economists estimate that Marshall aid contributed less than 5 per cent of West German national income, and Britain received twice as much. Erhard's reforms and good industrial relations are now seen as more important.

This mattered because rapid growth gave the new democracy jobs and goods, which meant that West Germans came to associate democracy with prosperity, unlike in the Weimar years.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The social market economy produced rapid growth.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Unemployment was over 10 per cent in 1951.
It applied first only to heavy industry.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Marshall aid was less decisive than once thought.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Layton and Fulbrook stress its importance.

chunks.title: Housing, refugees, welfare and education
chunks.body:
The social market economy also had social aims. The most urgent was **housing**. With cities in ruins and millions of refugees, the state and private builders together built a million new homes by the mid-1950s, and six million new flats in the decade from 1950, more than half of them social housing. Erhard introduced strict rent controls and tenants' rights.

The integration of almost **nine million refugees** and expellees from the East was a remarkable achievement. A booming economy absorbed them, which smoothed differences of class and religion and weakened radical nationalist parties. Unemployment benefit, sickness and accident insurance and child benefit were introduced. By 1955 unemployment had fallen to about one million, the start of near full employment that lasted until the 1970s.

The cornerstone of welfare was the **Dynamic Pension** of 1957, which linked old-age pensions to wages, so that pensioners could maintain their standard of living. Economists called it "the most important social reform of the 1950s". West Germany did not follow Britain in creating a tax-funded National Health Service; health care remained based on insurance and run largely by the medical profession.

**Education** was left to the Länder, a reaction against the centralised Nazi system, which produced differing school systems. Reforms in 1953 and the Düsseldorf Agreement of 1955 standardised examinations, and by 1960 school fees had been abolished. But universities remained largely the preserve of an academic elite.

This mattered because welfare was tied to work and growth, which meant that the system rewarded those in employment and expanded only as fast as the economy did.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Housing policy met an acute shortage.
The Dynamic Pension was the key welfare reform.

chunks.title: Women and the victims of Nazism
chunks.body:
The Basic Law of 1949 declared that **men and women were equal**. Yet policy assumed a male breadwinner. Women could be dismissed from the civil service when they married, and an equality law of the late 1950s was needed before a wife could take a job without her husband's permission or keep control of her property. Women's average pay remained 40 per cent below men's. The share of women entering higher education rose from 19 per cent in 1949 to about a third by the late 1960s, and the 1954 Weisser Report presented working women as a positive model. But even in the 1980s women were only just over 10 per cent of Bundestag members. Mary Fulbrook notes that women remained concentrated in lower-status, less well-paid, part-time or temporary work.

Policy towards the **victims of Nazism** was selective. The Basic Law granted automatic citizenship to those persecuted by the Nazis. In September 1951 Adenauer acknowledged "the immeasurable suffering endured by the Jews", and under the **Luxembourg Agreement** of September 1952 West Germany agreed to pay Israel three billion marks and a further 450 million marks to Jewish organisations. Other victims were treated very differently. In 1950 judges in Baden-Württemberg were told that Sinti and Roma had been persecuted "not for any racial reason" but for an "asocial and criminal record", so most had little hope of compensation. The Federal Republic kept Paragraph 175, which criminalised sex between men in the form Hitler had broadened; about 100,000 men faced court cases between 1945 and 1969.

This mattered because the new democracy promised equal rights in law but applied them unevenly in practice, which meant that equality for women and recognition for some victims came only slowly.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Legal equality for women was not matched in practice.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Women's access to higher education grew.
Money could not compensate for lives.
The Basic Law promised equal rights.

chunks.title: Wealth, guest workers and the costs of unity
chunks.body:
Did prosperity mean equality? Bottaro and Stanley suggest that wealth became more widely shared, not by narrowing the income gap, but by bringing more people into the middle class. In 1955 many still lived modestly: a third of Germans had never had a holiday, only 10 per cent owned a fridge and half lived in one-bedroom flats. And by 1959, 1.8 per cent of households controlled 35 per cent of private wealth.

Growth also created a demand for labour that West Germany met with **foreign workers**. By the peak year of 1973 there were 2.8 million, one in eight of the workforce, including 605,000 Turks. They had no permanent right of residence and were kept in entry-level jobs and wages. When recession came in 1974–75 they were the first to be laid off. In 1975 the Federal Republic closed its recruiting offices, and in 1977 a federal commission declared that "Germany is not an immigrant country".

The last great policy decision of the period came with unification. The **monetary, economic and social union** of 1 July 1990 allowed East Germans to exchange their marks, up to the equivalent of DM 40,000, at 1:1, and paid East German wages in Deutschmarks at parity. It kept East Germans from moving west, but Judt notes that it had grim long-term consequences for East German jobs and for the West German budget.

This mattered because West German prosperity rested partly on people who did not fully share in it, which meant that the limits of the social market economy showed most clearly at its edges: among guest workers, and in the East after 1990.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: More people joined the middle class.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Guest workers met labour demand without equal rights.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: They earned far more than at home.
It kept East Germans at home.

modelPlan.thesis: Foreign workers were recruited because near full employment created a labour shortage; the results were faster growth but a large population without full rights, the first to lose jobs in the recession of 1974–75.

arguments.claim: Result: lay-offs and the end of recruitment.

modelPlan.counter: Guest workers earned many times what they could at home, which suggests benefits for them too.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which result mattered most? A permanent population treated as temporary.

segments.text: Foreign workers were recruited because the economic miracle created a shortage of labour.
By 1955 unemployment had fallen to about one million, and by 1973 there were 2.8 million foreign workers, one in eight of the labour force.
This meant that West Germany gained a flexible workforce, so guest workers were kept at entry-level jobs and were the first laid off in 1974–75.
However, many stayed, while a 1977 commission insisted that 'Germany is not an immigrant country'.
The most significant result was therefore a large population whose position policy refused to recognise.

essayQuestions.text: Analyse the policies of the Federal Republic towards victims of Nazi persecution between 1949 and 1969.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which groups gained, which did not, and why?

modelPlan.thesis: The Federal Republic made substantial restitution to Jews and Israel, but denied recognition to Sinti and Roma and continued to prosecute gay men, which shows a selective approach to the Nazi past.
modelPlan.counter: Jewish delegations argued that no material restitution could compensate for lost lives.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Why selective? Restitution to Jews was tied to Western acceptance; other victims had no such advocates.

segments.text: The Federal Republic's policy towards victims of Nazism was generous to some and harsh to others.
Under the Luxembourg Agreement of 1952 it agreed to pay Israel three billion marks, yet a 1950 directive in Baden-Württemberg denied that Sinti and Roma had suffered racial persecution.
This meant that restitution depended on which victims West Germany and its Western partners recognised, so Sinti and Roma had little hope of redress.
However, the Basic Law did give automatic citizenship to all those persecuted by the Nazis, regardless of group.
The policy was therefore selective, shaped by politics as much as by justice.

essayQuestions.text: To what extent did economic recovery lead to a more equal distribution of wealth in West Germany between 1949 and 1960?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far

modelPlan.thesis: Recovery spread prosperity more widely, bringing more people into the middle class and paying for housing and pensions, but it did not narrow inequality: wealth remained highly concentrated.
modelPlan.counter: In 1955 a third of Germans had never had a holiday and only 10 per cent owned a fridge.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: More equal? More widely shared, but not more evenly distributed.

segments.text: Economic recovery spread prosperity but did not make West Germany more equal.
Growth paid for six million new flats and the Dynamic Pension, yet by 1959 1.8 per cent of households controlled 35 per cent of private wealth.
This meant that more people joined the middle class while the richest kept a large share, so the gap at the top remained.
However, Bottaro and Stanley note that class gaps seemed narrower as more ordinary people shared in Erhard's social economy.
Recovery therefore widened access to prosperity but did not produce a more equal distribution of wealth.
